desc:
Convert the 32-bit signed integer num to its hexadecimal representation and return it as a string of lowercase digits 0-9a-f.

  • The result has no leading zeros, except that zero itself is "0".
  • A negative number is written with its 32-bit two's complement representation, so -1 becomes "ffffffff" (eight digits).

Do not use a built-in conversion such as hex() or a format specifier; extract the digits yourself.

Examples: 26 gives "1a", -1 gives "ffffffff", -2147483648 gives "80000000".
hints: One hexadecimal digit stores exactly 4 bits, so you can read the number 4 bits at a time with a mask.
num & 15 is the lowest hex digit and num >> 4 drops it. Repeat until the number is 0, then reverse the collected digits.
For negative numbers, add 232 first (or mask with 0xFFFFFFFF). That gives the two's complement bit pattern as a non-negative value, and the same loop works.
editorial: A 32-bit two's complement pattern of a negative number x is the unsigned value x + 232. After that mapping the problem is plain base-16 conversion of a non-negative number: repeatedly take the low four bits with & 15, look up the digit character and shift right by four.

Digits come out from least to most significant, so reverse them at the end. Zero needs a special case because the loop would produce no digits. There are at most eight digits, so the work is constant. In languages with fixed-width integers use an unsigned shift (or mask) to avoid sign extension looping forever on negative values.
